newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech stock mkt discounts govt confidence vote win.
newsitem.headline: Czech stock mkt discounts govt confidence vote win.

text.p: Czech shares posted moderate gains in relatively heavy trading on Monday as the market discounted a government victory in Tuesday's parliamentary confidence vote, dealers said.
The official PX50 index closed up 3.8 points, 0.8 pct, to 501.4 with turnover rising to 1.3 billion crowns.

On Tuesday, Parliament will vote on a motion of confidence in the centre-right coalition government which was called by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus after after two weeks of turbulence in the foreign exchange markets rattled the government and led to the resignation of three senior minsters.
"There has already been demonstrated a fairly strong impact on the market which has already discounted a positive outcome for the government," said Radek Vavra of Citicorp Securities.
Vavra said that the optimism had been reflected not only in rising prices, but also in greater volumes, which he said were particularly evident on the over-the-counter (OTC) market.
"It (optimism) is also reflected in volumes. In the OTC market we're seeing good lots of shares."
On Monday, most major issues closed higher. SPT Telecom rose 24 crowns to 3,219, power utility CEZ edged up crowns to 901 and Komercni Banka gained 55 crowns to 2,000.

Ivan Kusacek of Zivnostenska Banka agreed with Vavra's view that there was a speculative element involved in Monday's gains but questioned whether a victory for the coalition would be sufficient to bring foreign investors back.
"Foreign investors are still really waiting for better macro-economic indicators," he said.
"The first step is that the political situation should stabilise but if the government gets through I don't think foreign investors will heavily buy Czech stocks," added Kusacek.
All dealers polled by Reuters on Monday expected the government to win the confidence vote and said that a defeat would be received very badly by the market.
"I don't think it would be viewed (by the market) as good...it will bring uncertainty to the market," said Lubomir Vystavel of ING Barings.
